snippet.title: Software Engineers Are Becoming Supervisors, Not Coders
snippet.description:
The role of the software engineer is shifting from producer to supervisor in 2026. You're no longer responsible for writing massive amounts of code by hand — AI code generation has gotten so good that not using it means falling behind the developers who do. 

So yes, you'll AI-generate a lot of your code. But the skill that actually matters now is judgment: understanding what good code looks like, what's bad, and what's maintainable for the future. 

Anyone can generate code. Knowing what to keep is the real edge.

snippet.title: What Separates a Side Project From a Real AI Product
snippet.description:
The most valuable AI engineering skill most people skip — and the one employers actually want. Building a cool AI demo on your laptop is easy. Running it in production, where real users depend on it, is a completely different challenge.

To ship a real AI product you need to understand rate limiting, because these APIs have hard limits you can't blow past. You need caching, because every API call costs money and you don't want to pay thousands for the same responses. 

You need monitoring, so you know the moment your app breaks. And you need cost management, because LLM API bills spiral out of control fast. That's what separates a side project from a real product.

snippet.title: AI Engineer Myths Debunked
snippet.description:
Is AI engineering a completely different discipline from software engineering? Not really — it's a specialization within it. If you want to be a good AI engineer, most of your job is traditional software engineering work that just happens to interact with an AI model at some point. 

So if you're thinking becoming an AI engineer means you can skip all the software engineering fundamentals, that's completely wrong. You still need to set up APIs, build backend services, write tests, do code reviews, and manage deployments. 

The AI part sits on top of real engineering skills.

snippet.title: It's Been a Good Run, ISPs.
snippet.description:
That escalated quickly...

In my last video, I introduced Reticulum—an open-source protocol that could allow anyone to build networks without relying on traditional internet infrastructure. But there was one big question left unanswered: how far can it actually go?

In this video, I start with a simple setup inside my house and begin pushing the limits—testing communication across rooms, neighborhoods, and beyond using WiFi HaLow and mesh networking. The goal is simple: see if it’s possible to send real messages across distance without depending on ISPs, centralized servers, or the internet as we know it.

Reticulum routes traffic above the radio layer, automatically bridging dissimilar frequencies, interfaces, and modulation types. I then run it over Wi-Fi HaLow Haven nodes to create a long-range, encrypted IP mesh with no traditional infrastructure. Finally, I push it further by running ATAK across the network, demonstrating a fully open-source, decentralized communication stack in action.

snippet.title: How To Use LTspice, A Free Circuit Simulator
snippet.description:
This tutorial shows how to use LTspice, which is a powerful, open-source circuit simulator. It starts out by drawing a simple circuit with a voltage source, resistor, LED, and ground. A custom model is made for the LED. Next, a full adder is built at the transistor level using NAND logic gates. The full adder is turned into a symbol so a 4-bit calculator can be stimulated. Finally, an astable multivibrator output is simulated and compared to values measured on an oscilloscope and values found using EasyEDA. Both an operating point simulation and a transient simulation will be used.

snippet.title: Neural Networks, From First Principals, A Single Perceptron.
snippet.description:
Understanding the fundamentals of neural networks is very important. For this reason, understanding how a single perception works is a good place to start. 

A single perception can separate two linearly separable classes in 2D or 3D. This is done but using the perception learning algorithm, which is also called the perception learning rule, or just the delta rule. 

When a given x1 and x1 input is given the perception can predict whether the output is going to be class 1 or class 2. If there is an error the weights and bias can be adjusted in a direction that will reduce the error. This is done over multiple epochs until the network is trained. 

An example of a perceptron separating two classes of data is provided in 2D and 3D. This is done using the step activation function. An in-depth discussion about how the boundary layer gets adjusted is provided. We then look at how a single perceptron can solve some logic gate cases such as the AND, OR NAND, and NOR Gates. However, a multi-layer neural network will be needed to solve the XOR and XNOR cases.

snippet.description:

But companies still test the way they did 5-8 years ago: LeetCode-style interviews, six or seven rounds, whiteboard coding. The result is that genuinely great developers who can build real applications get filtered out simply because they didn't grind LeetCode for three months. 

Here's why the way we hire engineers needs to catch up to the way the job actually works now.

snippet.description:
Run your own always-on Claude Code agent on a VPS:
https://www.hostinger.com/teacherstech
Use code TEACHERSTECH for 10% off your Claude Code VPS plan. 

Set it up once and your agent keeps coding 24/7, even with your laptop closed.
 
Claude Code can already be controlled from your phone, but the session dies the moment your laptop goes to sleep. In this video I will show you how to run Claude Code on an always-on Hostinger VPS, so your coding tasks keep grinding 24/7 even when you are away from your desk.
 
Claude Code's Remote Control feature lets you drive a coding session from your phone or browser, but it only stays alive as long as your computer does. Running Claude Code on a VPS fixes that by giving it a dedicated, always-on server that never sleeps. In this beginner-friendly walkthrough you will see how to set up a Hostinger VPS with the Claude Code template, secure it, connect over SSH, keep your session alive with tmux, and control it from the Claude app on your phone. I will also run two real demos: fixing a bug from my phone while the laptop is closed, and kicking off a full code migration that finishes on its own. By the end you will know exactly how to set up your own always-on Claude Code agent.
